prompt:
I need the front end for Peakmind. An electricity-demand watcher for owner-run craft studios and small workshops on commercial utility rates, which follows their meter readings and equipment use and warns them before they set a costly new peak-demand charge.

Who's using it: Ines Calderón, a self-employed potter who runs a one-woman ceramics studio in a rented industrial unit on a small-commercial electric rate. Two electric kilns are her biggest power draw. Last winter, one badly timed firing during a utility peak event added $410 to a single bill, so she wants to know early, not after the fact.

What they're doing right now: It's Monday afternoon and Ines has a glaze firing scheduled to start at 4:30 pm in the big kiln, while the small kiln is already partway through a bisque firing. The utility just announced a peak-demand event for 5–8 pm tomorrow. She needs to see how close this month's demand already is to her billing peak, whether running both kilns together this evening would set a new one, and set things up so she's alerted only if demand is about to cross the line, not every time a kiln clicks on. Then she'll decide whether to delay the glaze firing.

What's in the system at this point: Smart-meter readings in 15-minute intervals since Oct 28 (the billing cycle start), about 1,830 readings in kW and kWh. Rate: Small Commercial TOU-B, with on-peak 4–9 pm weekdays at $0.31/kWh, off-peak at $0.14/kWh and a demand charge of $18.40 per kW of the cycle's highest 15-minute demand. Current cycle peak: 21.6 kW (Nov 4, 6:15 pm). Equipment: Big kiln (L&L-style 240 V, about 11.5 kW), Small kiln (about 7.2 kW, bisque cycle 9 hours, started 9:40 am, now at 1,420 °F), pug mill 1.5 kW, heater 2 kW, studio lights 0.8 kW. Planned firings: glaze cone 6 in the Big kiln, Nov 16 at 4:30 pm, about 10 hours. Utility notices: peak event Tue Nov 17, 5–8 pm. Ines's current alert rules: notify at 18 kW (too noisy, 23 alerts last month), and a utility event notice. Bill history for the last 12 months: $186–$612.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
